cards.explanation: The answer is True. David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), prays, “Do not let me be put to shame…” in verse 2. He adds a second request right behind it, that his enemies not exult over him. Two asks in one verse, and not a single wasted word.
The answer is False. David says, “Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame…” None means none, friends. He isn't leaving a little side door open for an exception.

The answer is people who betray without cause. Verse 3 says “…those who engage in treachery without cause will be disgraced.” Treachery is betrayal, and the words without cause matter, because this is betrayal that had no reason behind it. David puts that group right next to those who wait for the LORD, and they land in opposite places.

The answer is that the LORD is the God of his salvation. Verse 5 says, “Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation…” David's reason isn't about himself at all. It's about who the LORD is to him. He asks for a guide because he knows whose hand he's holding.
The answer is day. Verse 5 says, “all day long I wait for You.” That's the whole day spent waiting, friends. I'd be checking my oven timer every two minutes.

The answer is the LORD's compassion and loving devotion. Verse 6 says, “Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and loving devotion, for they are from age to age.” David isn't handing the LORD a list of things he's done. He's pointing at what the LORD is like, and says it lasts from age to age.

The answer is False. Verse 7 has David asking, “Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts…” So he asks the LORD not to remember them. Then he asks to be remembered according to the LORD's loving devotion instead.

The answer is sinners. Verse 8 says, “Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way.” Read that slowly, friends. The LORD's goodness is the reason He shows sinners the way. I'd say that's good news for every one of us who's ever had a rough batch.
The answer is True. Verse 9 says, “He guides the humble in what is right and teaches them His way.” Notice there are two parts there, guiding and teaching, friends. It's the LORD doing both.

The answer is those who keep His covenant and decrees. Verse 10 says, “All the LORD’s ways are loving and faithful to those who keep His covenant and His decrees.” Loving AND faithful, both at once. You know that friend who's super sweet but never shows up? Not the same thing, and David names exactly who gets both.

The answer is False. In verse 11 David says, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, forgive my iniquity, for it is great.” He calls it great, with no dressing it up. And he asks for forgiveness anyway, for the sake of the LORD's name.

The answer is that the LORD will instruct him in the path chosen for him. Verse 12 says, “Who is the man who fears the LORD? He will instruct him in the path chosen for him.” So the LORD does the teaching, and there's a path chosen for that man. That's a whole lot better than winging it and hoping for the best.

The answer is descendants. Verse 13 says, “His soul will dwell in prosperity, and his descendants will inherit the land.” So it reaches past the man himself, on to his descendants. That's a blessing with a long line behind it.

The answer is True. Verse 15 says, “My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh.” That little word for gives the reason, friends. David looks to the LORD because of what he says the LORD will do.

The answer is that he is lonely and afflicted. Verse 16 says, “Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted.” David gives no fancy reason, just where he is. I think it takes some courage to say lonely out loud to the LORD.

The answer is False. Verse 17 says, “The troubles of my heart increase; free me from my distress.” They're growing, not shrinking. I think this is a heavy spot in the psalm, and David doesn't hide it.

The answer is sins. Verse 18 says, “Consider my affliction and trouble, and take away all my sins.” Notice it's all my sins, and it comes right alongside his trouble. David brings the whole load at once.

The answer is False. Verse 19 says, “Consider my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with vicious hatred.” So they're many, not a few. David gives it to the LORD straight, which I think takes some courage.

The answer is that he takes refuge in the LORD. Verse 20 says, “Guard my soul and deliver me; let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in You.” His reason is where he runs to, not what he's done. It's a short sentence with a lot of room in it.

The answer is True. Verse 21 says, “May integrity and uprightness preserve me, because I wait for You.” He asks for integrity and uprightness to preserve him, and he gives his waiting on the LORD as the reason. Waiting and integrity in one breath, friends, and I bet that's not easy to hold together.

The answer is Israel. The very last line, verse 22, says, “Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress.” After all that talk of his own trouble, David ends with a prayer for the whole people. That's a big finish.
